Which West Union office takes a deed for Adams County land?

Deeds and mortgages for Adams County property go to the county recorder in West Union, at 110 West Main Street, Room 133, West Union, OH 45693. The county's recorder page prints two phone lines, 937-544-5051 and 937-544-2513, and a Monday to Friday schedule that closes at 4 in the afternoon.

Records can also be searched through the Adams County public access portal. The portal asks for a username and password, so plan to create an account before you try a search. It also promotes a real estate transfer alert service that flags new filings. The portal's banner frames the alerts as protection against real estate fraud.

What fee schedule does Ohio impose on an Adams County filing?

Ohio sets recording fees by statute, so the Adams County counter cannot negotiate them. Section 317.32 of the Revised Code splits each charge into a base fee and a housing trust fund fee of the same size. On an ordinary instrument, pages one and two cost $17 plus $17 together, and each sheet after that (legal size, or any fraction of one, with the caption page counted) costs $4 plus $4.

The section also authorizes a document preservation surcharge, capped at $5 per instrument and paid into the county general fund. Because the statute sets only a ceiling, ask the recorder which figure Adams County applies before you write the check.

Fees are collected at the counter when you hand the paper in. Electronic filers may settle afterward by electronic funds transfer, automated clearing house or a similar method.

What happens at the auditor's office before the recorder takes the deed?

In Ohio the deed stops at the county auditor first. Under section 319.202, whoever is taking title (or that person's representative) files a statement of value, either electronically or as three paper copies, and the auditor endorses the deed with the fee charged and a note that the filing was made. The deed then goes to the recorder's window.

The seller pays two possible charges to the auditor at that stage:

  • The state-authorized conveyance fee in section 319.54(G)(3), which comes to $1 or ten cents for each hundred dollars of value (counting a partial hundred as a full one), whichever is larger.
  • A county real property transfer tax, but only where the commissioners have adopted one under section 322.02, limited to thirty cents on each hundred dollars and charged to the grantor.

Phone the auditor at 937-544-2364 to learn whether Adams County levies the optional tax. The county offices directory also lists the treasurer at 937-544-2317, the commissioners at 937-544-3286 and the clerk of courts title department at 937-544-2345.

Which Adams County transfers skip the conveyance fee?

Several family and court transfers are carved out of the auditor's fee in section 319.54(G)(3). The ones a seller or heir meets most often are these:

  • A gift between spouses, or from a parent to a child or to the child's spouse.
  • A deed whose only job is to fix or confirm one already on record.
  • A transfer made only to pledge property for a debt or to lift that pledge.
  • Property passing among the heirs or devisees of the same decedent with no money paid for it.
  • A deed into a trust whose maker kept an unlimited power to revoke it.
  • A transaction with no money or other valuable consideration that also is not a gift.
  • An interest valued at $100 or less.

When an exemption applies, the filing has to state the reason for it.

What does the seller have to disclose on the statement of value?

Section 319.202 ties the deed filing to the property tax bill. The buyer's statement either affirms that the seller said the preceding or current year's taxes will not be reduced under section 323.152 , or it comes with a sworn instrument giving the estimated reduction. If the property has farm-use valuation, a similar affirmation covers the current agricultural use value and any recoupment charge.

Before closing, find out which reductions your parcel carries. The auditor's office can tell you, and the county directory gives the same 937-544-2364 number for CAUV farm valuation questions.

How big is Adams County and what are its homes like?

Adams County spreads across 586 square miles of southern Ohio, and West Union is both the seat and the biggest village. Neighbors are Highland, Pike, Scioto and Brown counties, and across the river lie Lewis and Mason counties in Kentucky. Villages include Manchester, Peebles, Rome, Seaman and Winchester, and fifteen townships fill the rest, from Bratton and Brush Creek to Tiffin and Wayne. The Great Serpent Mound at Locust Grove draws visitors, and Shawnee State Park and the Edge of Appalachia Preserve sit inside the county lines.

  • Population: 27,865 in July 2025, a gain of 1.4 percent over the 2020 census base.
  • Housing units: 12,808, with an owner-occupancy rate of 71.7 percent for 2020 to 2024.
  • Typical home value: $164,200, the Census median for houses their owners live in.
  • Median gross rent: $732 a month.
  • Household income: $50,264 at the median, and the average worker travels 36.4 minutes to a job.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts supply these numbers and also shows 20 building permits for 2025. The county has about 47 residents per square mile. Ask the recorder how many pages your deed runs, since each page past the second adds to the fee.

How should an Adams County owner handle a quick sale?

A sale to a cash buyer follows the usual route: a deed, a statement of value at the auditor, then recording at the West Union counter. A closing agent or title company usually carries the paperwork between those two offices. If you handle it without an agent, ask the auditor about the conveyance fee and any optional county tax first, then ask the recorder for the page rate and surcharge.

Inherited houses add steps, because the person signing must have authority over the estate. Heirs should check with the court that handles the estate before signing a deed, and ask the title agent what proof the recorder will want attached.

More questions about Adams County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How do I reach the Adams County recorder by phone?

Call 937-544-5051 or 937-544-2513, the two lines on the recorder's page. The counter is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. at 110 West Main Street, Room 133, in West Union.

What will the Adams County recorder charge to file a deed?

Ohio Revised Code 317.32 sets $17 plus a matching $17 housing trust fund fee for pages one and two, then $4 plus $4 per added page. A county surcharge of up to $5 may sit on top, so get the final total from the recorder.

Is there a county transfer tax on an Adams County sale?

The statewide conveyance fee reaches most sales. An extra county tax exists only if the commissioners adopted one, so ask the auditor at 937-544-2364 whether Adams County did.

Which side files the statement of value on an Adams County sale?

The person taking title, or a representative, files it with the auditor, electronically or in three paper copies. The seller pays the conveyance fee and any county tax at that point.

Is a deed from parent to child exempt from the conveyance fee in Adams County?

Generally yes. Gifts from a parent to a child or the child's spouse appear on the exemption list in section 319.54(G)(3), but the filing must give the reason and recording fees still apply.

Where is the Allen County recorder's office in Lima?

The Allen County Recorder works from 237 N. Main St., Suite 132, Lima, OH 45801, in the building the treasurer's page calls the Allen Government Center, next to the courthouse. The recorder's page gives the phone as (419) 223-8517 and a mailing box at P.O. Box 1243, Lima, OH 45802. Posted hours run Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., with the counter closed from 11:00 a.m. to noon for lunch.

That lunch closure matters if you plan to hand a deed over at midday. Mailed documents have a rule of their own, covered below.

What documents does the Allen County recorder keep?

The office describes itself as the county's permanent keeper of land records, and it indexes each document so a title examiner can trace a chain of ownership. Its list of holdings is wider than most sellers expect:

  • Deeds and mortgages, plus a daily register of both that the public may read during business hours.
  • Liens against property for delinquent taxes.
  • Maps, plats of town lots and other land divisions, and the property lines recorded for the county.
  • Powers of attorney.
  • Military service discharges, which are recorded without a fee.

The office will furnish a certified copy of any record on request and payment of the fee, and it charges by the number of pages. It also warns that a recorder can be sued on the official bond for failing to record a document or for damaging a record.

What are the rules for mailing or e-recording a deed in Allen County?

Mail submissions come with one firm condition. The recorder accepts a conveyance by mail only if the Allen County Auditor's conveyance stamp is already on it. A deed that skips the auditor first goes nowhere, so stop at the auditor before you stamp an envelope.

Electronic recording needs setup in advance:

  • Open an escrow account with the office.
  • File a completed e-Recording agreement, which the recorder's page offers for download and which is mailed to the recorder's Main Street address.
  • Expect a possible fee from the e-recording vendor on top of the county's recording charge.

One more screen applies to every route. Under ORC 317.082, as the office's page puts it, the recorder will not accept a document that contains a Social Security number unless an affidavit is attached or the document is one the law excludes. Redact the number before you bring a deed in.

How much does recording cost in Allen County?

The recorder's page says the fee for each class of document is set by law and tells filers to consult the Revised Code. That law is section 317.32. For an ordinary instrument it prints a base fee of $17 and a housing trust fund fee of $17 for the first two pages, then $4 and $4 for each further page, and it allows a preservation surcharge of up to $5 that goes to the county general fund.

A few other items in that section matter to a seller: certification of a copy is $1 plus $1 per page, and filing an instrument that marks a marginal reference is $2 plus $2 per reference. The office's own printable fee schedule is linked from its page, so use that sheet for the exact total for your documents.

What does the Allen County auditor charge before a deed is recorded?

The auditor's FAQ page answers this directly: the conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand of the purchase price, and the transfer charge is $.50 per parcel. Checks for the auditor's fees are written to the Allen County Auditor. The same page says a conveyance form from another Ohio county is acceptable as long as it has four parts.

The auditor's side also decides what a buyer inherits. Allen County taxes follow ownership, and the auditor does not prorate them, so the split between seller and buyer belongs on the closing statement. A parcel is billed as it stood on January 1, so ask for a tax split request if you are dividing land.

A sale touches three desks at the Allen Government Center and nearby. Each prints its own contact details, gathered here for one trip.

TreasurerCollects real estate tax and sewer bills237 N Main St, Suite 123; (419) 223-8515; weekdays 8:00 to 4:30

The auditor's site lists a property search, a tax calculator, a property sales lookup, maps, and pages for CAUV farm valuation and the Allen County Land Bank. Ask the auditor whether a county transfer tax applies to your deed, since that depends on a commissioners' resolution under section 322.02 that sets a ceiling of 30 cents per $100.

What is Allen County like for someone selling a house?

Allen County sits in northwest Ohio, created by the legislature on March 1, 1820 and organized in 1831. It is named for Colonel John Allen, who died at the Battle of Frenchtown in the War of 1812. Lima is both the county seat and the largest city, and the city of Delphos lies partly inside the county. Villages include Beaverdam, Bluffton (in part), Cairo, Elida, Harrod, Lafayette and Spencerville. An 1885 oil discovery in Lima started a boom that lasted past 1910, and the county fair has run every August in Lima since 1851.

  • Population: 100,881 in July 2025, down 1.3 percent from the April 2020 base.
  • Housing units: 44,946, with 67.7 percent owner-occupied in 2020 to 2024.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $165,300.
  • Land area: 402.55 square miles, about 254 residents per square mile in 2020.

Those numbers come from the Census Bureau. Neighbors are Putnam, Hancock, Hardin, Auglaize and Van Wert counties, and the Lima Allen County Airport lies about five nautical miles southeast of downtown Lima.

What should an owner do before selling an Allen County house?

Work in this order: confirm who is on title, call the treasurer about any balance, get the auditor's stamp, then record. A closing agent normally handles the last two steps. If you handle them yourself, bring a deed with no Social Security number on it.

Families who inherit a house should ask the probate court which papers support a deed. Selling a house with open repairs or a tenant does not change the recording steps, although a mortgage payoff will add a release for the recorder to file.

More questions about Allen County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Does the Allen County recorder close for lunch?

Yes. The posted schedule is Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., with the office closed from 11:00 a.m. to noon.

Can I mail a deed to the Allen County recorder?

Yes, but only if the Allen County Auditor's conveyance stamp is already on it. Without the stamp the recorder does not accept a mailed conveyance.

Does Allen County accept electronic recording?

It does for filers who set up an escrow account and file a completed e-Recording agreement. The e-recording vendor may charge its own fee.

Are military discharge records free to record in Allen County?

Yes. The recorder's page states that there is no fee for recording military service discharges.

Why was my deed refused for a Social Security number?

Ohio Revised Code 317.082 bars the recorder from accepting a document that contains one unless an affidavit is attached or the document is excluded by law. Black the number out of the copy you submit, or ask the closing agent how the office wants it handled.

Belmont County by the numbers

Who records a deed in Belmont County, Ohio?

Deeds, mortgages and related papers in Belmont County are filed with the recorder, whose office is in the St. Clairsville courthouse, 101 West Main Street. The recorder describes the job as keeping the county's land records accurate, indexed and open to the public, with more than 220 years of them on hand. Staff can explain how the records are arranged, but a title search is something you arrange separately.

Indexing is the part sellers rarely notice. Each document is indexed so that a searcher can build a chain of title, which shows every owner and every debt attached to the land. Accurate indexing is what lets a title searcher find a deed, a lien or a release later.

Belmont County was organized in November 1801 and named St. Clairsville its seat in 1803, so the books reach back more than two centuries. Wikipedia places the county along the Ohio River, and the recorder's own description of the work includes farm deeds, home mortgages, oil and gas leases and military discharge papers.

What does Belmont County charge to put a document on record?

The recorder's online calculator states a simple structure that follows Ohio Revised Code 317.32. Belmont County does not add the optional $5 document preservation fee, which the statute lets a county charge.

Belmont County Recorder fee structure
ServiceFee
First two pages of a document$34
Each additional page$8
Each indexed marginal notation (reference)$4
Document that misses the layout standard$20 extra

Source: Belmont County Recorder fee calculator.

In the statute, the first two pages carry a $17 base fee and a second $17 for the housing trust fund. Each added page carries a $4 base and a $4 trust fund share. The statute sends any preservation surcharge to the county general fund, and the trust fund share is collected under section 317.36. Other services carry their own statutory rates:

  • Certified copy: a $1 base fee and a $1 trust fund fee per page, plus 50 cents and 50 cents when the recorder's seal is needed.
  • Photocopy at the counter: $1 and $1 per page.
  • Each marginal reference: $2 and $2, which matches the $4 in the table.
  • Living will or health care power of attorney: a base fee of $17 to $20 plus a matching trust fund fee.

Payment is due when the paper is handed in, except that electronic filers may settle by funds transfer or ACH afterward. The calculator is the quickest way to price a deed with several pages of legal description.

What layout rules apply to a deed recorded in Belmont County?

Documents must meet the standards in section 317.114, which the recorder summarizes on its document standards page. A document that falls short is still recorded, with a $20 surcharge.

  • Text set in at least 10-point type.
  • Sheets between letter size (8 1/2 by 11) and legal size (8 1/2 by 14).
  • Ink in black or blue, with highlighter left off the page.
  • Three inches of blank space above the text on page one, then an inch and a half on each page after.
  • One inch free along both sides and the bottom edge.

The rules do not apply to papers from a court or taxing authority, plats, exhibits, DD-214 discharge papers, state or federal documents, or any document signed before the law took effect in July 2009.

What documents does a Belmont County recorder have to file?

Section 317.08 lists what goes into the official records, and the list explains why more than deeds pass through the counter. Items most relevant to a house sale include:

  • Deeds and other instruments that convey land outright.
  • Mortgages, with their amendments, modifications and extensions.
  • Executory installment contracts for land that run more than a year.
  • Options to purchase, which must state a specific day and year of expiration.
  • Powers of attorney and memoranda of trust.
  • Declarations and bylaws for condominiums under Chapter 5311.
  • Easements, environmental covenants and conservation easements under the listed statutes.

For a seller the important point is that a recorded mortgage, option or contract stays in the public record until a release or other instrument is recorded against it. Ask a title company to check the county's records for a paid-off mortgage whose release was never recorded.

What happens before the recorder sees a Belmont County deed?

The auditor's office sits in the same courthouse and acts on the deed. Under section 319.202, the auditor does not endorse a deed until the grantee or a representative submits a statement declaring the value of the property, or a statement of the reason for exemption. The deed transfer desk takes calls at 740-699-2136, and the real estate desk at 740-699-2132.

A common order in Ohio counties, which Belmont County's offices can confirm, runs like this:

  • Draft the deed with the legal description and parcel number.
  • Take the deed and value statement to the auditor, pay the conveyance fee and get the endorsement.
  • Present the endorsed deed to the recorder with the fee.
  • Receive the recorded original or a return by mail.

Ask the auditor's deed transfer desk for the current conveyance rate, since counties set their own transfer tax within the limit in the statute. Ask the recorder's staff whether the recorded deed can be returned by mail.

What does the local market mean for a Belmont County seller?

In the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures, the typical owned home is valued at $154,900, and 73.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Nearly 91 percent of residents (90.9 percent) were in the same house a year earlier, so title often sits unchanged for years and older deeds are common. The 2020 census counted 31,618 housing units, and 13.6 percent of them stood vacant. Owners spend a median $1,215 a month with a mortgage and $489 without one. People 65 and older make up 24.9 percent of the population.

Estimated population slipped 3.1 percent from the April 2020 base to July 2025. The county's protected areas include Barkcamp State Park, Dysart Woods and the Egypt Valley Wildlife Area, and its lakes include Piedmont Lake and Belmont Lake. A house near any of them is sold on the same recorded title as one in town.

If a deed has gaps, such as a missing heir or a lien never released, the recorder cannot fix it. Clear it up through a title company or attorney before a new deed goes on record.

More questions about Belmont County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the price of recording a deed in Belmont County?

Per the recorder's calculator, the first two pages run $34 and every page after costs $8. A $4 fee applies to each indexed reference, and a document that misses the layout standard costs $20 more. The county does not add the optional $5 preservation fee.

Where is the Belmont County Recorder's office?

Find it inside the St. Clairsville courthouse (101 West Main Street, Ohio 43950), under the same roof as the auditor and treasurer. Deed transfers start at the auditor's desk, which takes calls at 740-699-2136.

What paper size and ink does the recorder require?

Print on letter or legal paper in black or blue ink, at 10 point or larger, with no highlighter. Keep the top margin at 3 inches on page one and 1 1/2 inches after that, and leave 1 inch at the sides and bottom. A document that misses these standards costs $20 more to record.

Does the recorder search my title?

No. The recorder's staff will explain how the records are arranged but will not perform title searches. Hire a title company or attorney for that, and expect a lender or buyer to ask for the result before closing.

Do I need the auditor before I record a Belmont County deed?

Yes, start with the auditor. The auditor's endorsement under section 319.202 depends on a statement of value, or a statement giving the reason for an exemption. Ask the recorder's staff how an endorsed deed should be delivered.

Brown County by the numbers

Where is Brown County, Ohio, and where do deeds get recorded?

Brown County lies along Ohio's southern boundary, where the Ohio River divides it from Kentucky. Georgetown is the county seat. The recorder works out of the Administration Building, 800 Mt. Orab Pike, Suite 151, Georgetown, Ohio 45121. The auditor (Suite 181) and treasurer (Suite 171) are in the same building.

Wikipedia gives 493 square miles and a creation date of March 1, 1818, cut from Adams and Clermont counties. Early settlers included the father of Ulysses S. Grant, who ran a tannery near Georgetown. Burley tobacco was first grown near Higginsport. Villages include Aberdeen, Fayetteville, Hamersville, Higginsport, Mount Orab, Ripley, Russellville and Sardinia, and Lake Waynoka and Lake Lorelei are census-designated places.

The Census Bureau counted 43,676 residents in 2020 and estimates 44,397 for July 2025. The Census QuickFacts table lists 19,965 housing units, with 77.2 percent lived in by owners and a median owned-home value of $196,200. The Census lists a 33.9-minute mean trip to work, and Wikipedia places the county in the Cincinnati metropolitan statistical area.

How much does the Brown County Recorder charge?

Per the recorder's fee page, the State of Ohio sets recording charges: half is the basic fee and half goes to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund (sections 317.32 and 317.36). Most common documents share one price.

Brown County Recorder fees for common documents

Source: Brown County Recorder fee page.

Federal tax liens cost $5.00 and releases $3.00. A living will or health care power of attorney is $40.00 to record, and one certified copy of a veteran's discharge is free. The page also links the Medicaid estate recovery notice of pending transfer of property.

What belongs on a Brown County deed before it is recorded?

The recorder's how-to page lists nine items that should be on a deed before it arrives:

  • The Tax Map office stamp approving the transfer.
  • The auditor's transfer endorsement.
  • The name of the seller.
  • The name and address of the buyer.
  • The seller's original signature and the date, with the name typed or printed beneath.
  • A notary acknowledgement.
  • A legal description naming the county, the township or village and the size of the land.
  • The parcel number.
  • A preparation statement.

The staff neither prepare documents nor sell forms, and legal advice is off the table. Most sellers have a title company or attorney draft it.

The fee page adds that a conveyance or exemption form is required with transfers and that parcel identification numbers are required on every deed. The non-standard fee applies unless a document has 10-point or larger type, letter or legal paper, black or blue ink and no highlighting, with 1-inch side and bottom margins and 3 inches at the top of the first page.

Which documents does the Brown County Recorder accept?

The recorder's document types page groups what the office handles. For a seller the relevant groups are:

  • Deeds: warranty, survivorship, quit claim and sheriff's deeds, and certificates of transfer.
  • Mortgages, with releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and amendments.
  • Land contracts, affidavits, easements and leases.
  • Plats and condominium drawings.
  • Powers of attorney, trusts and bills of sale.
  • Liens, including mechanic's liens, federal tax liens and homeowner association liens, along with notices of commencement.

The office also files military service discharges, zoning resolutions with maps, annexations and street name changes. Anything that touches a house sale and sits in the public record, from an old mortgage to a lien, was filed through this counter.

What is the order of offices for a Brown County deed?

The recorder's page sets out two routes, and on both the deed passes through the auditor and the county's Tax Map department.

  • In person. Start at the recorder's office, which checks the document for its own requirements and fees. Next go to the auditor's office next door to complete the conveyance. The Tax Map department then picks up the deed at the Engineer Building, 25 Veterans Blvd., Georgetown.
  • By mail. Send the deed to the recorder at the Suite 151 address with a cover note and a phone number, a check payable to Brown County Recorder, all auditor fees and forms, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Tax Map reviews documents in the order received, so the office says a deed cannot be walked through. Legal descriptions are checked there, and the recorder advises calling the department for its requirements. Once Tax Map and the auditor have stamped the deed, it returns to the recorder to be recorded. The auditor can answer questions at 937-378-6398.

What are the transfer fee and conveyance tax in Brown County?

Look to the recorder's fee page for the local number: $4.00 of transfer fee and conveyance tax on each $1,000 of purchase price, plus fifty cents per parcel number for the auditor. A conveyance or exemption form goes with every transfer.

Two statutes sit behind that figure. The auditor's statement-of-value fee is set in section 319.54(G)(3). Separately, section 322.02 allows a county to levy a deed transfer tax of no more than 30 cents per $100. The seller named in the deed owes that tax, and it is paid to the auditor before recording. Exempt transfers, such as family gifts, file an exemption statement rather than a value statement.

Ask the auditor which exemption box fits before you sign the deed.

How do taxes affect a Brown County sale?

Property tax is paid to the county treasurer (937-378-6705), whose weekday hours run 8:00 to 4:00. Brown County's 2025 real estate bills were payable February 11, 2026 and July 31, 2026. The later second-half date followed Ohio House Bill 186, which set up an inflation cap credit on certain school district levies and applied it back to tax year 2025.

The treasurer also handles payment plans for owners who fall behind, and runs a monthly escrow program that lets owners spread payments ahead of the bill. Online payment carries convenience fees, including $1.50 for an electronic check. The auditor's site lists 35,315 parcels in the county and notes that the homestead exemption, not any federal program, is the relief available to seniors, disabled owners and qualifying disabled veterans.

Have the title company get the parcel's balance from the treasurer before the closing date.

More questions about Brown County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the Brown County recording fee for a deed?

A deed of two pages or fewer is $39.00 on the fee page, and each added page or attachment is $8.00. Non-standard paper adds $20.00. The amounts come from section 317.32.

What is the mailing address for a Brown County deed?

Mail it to the Brown County Recorder, 800 Mt. Orab Pike, Suite 151, Georgetown, OH 45121. Include a cover note with your phone number, a check payable to Brown County Recorder, the auditor's fees and forms, and a stamped return envelope.

What is the conveyance tax in Brown County?

The page shows $4.00 per $1,000 of price, with the auditor's fifty-cent charge on each parcel number. Call the auditor at 937-378-6398 with questions, since the conveyance or exemption form must go with every transfer.

Does the Brown County Recorder prepare deeds?

No. Staff do not draft documents or sell forms, and they cannot advise on legal questions. A lawyer or title company drafts the deed. It then clears Tax Map and the auditor and only afterward reaches the recorder.

What were the 2026 Brown County tax due dates?

Real estate tax for 2025 was due February 11, 2026 (first half) and July 31, 2026 (second half, delayed because of House Bill 186). The treasurer's line, 937-378-6705, has the schedule for later years.

Which Hamilton office takes a Butler County deed?

Butler County keeps one recorder, and the counter sits at 130 High Street in Hamilton, OH 45011. Its fee schedule prints 513-887-3192 for the front desk, recorder@bcohio.gov for email, and a second number, 513-887-3154, for conveyance and transfer questions.

Sellers in Middletown, Fairfield, Oxford, Monroe, Trenton and Sharonville all file in that same building. The schedule promises a 24 hour turnaround and asks that every submission include a self addressed stamped return envelope. The recorder's website offers an online search of records from 1987 forward and carries the statutory warning that recorded papers are generally open to the public. Anything printed on a deed can be read by whoever searches for it, so leave off personal details the form does not require.

How much does the Butler County recorder charge on a deed?

Under the schedule effective January 1, 2025, a deed, mortgage or lease of up to two pages costs $39.00, a figure that already includes the $5.00 preservation surcharge. Every page past the second adds $8.00. Section 317.32 of the Revised Code is the source of the split: $17 base plus $17 for the housing trust fund on the first two pages, with the county free to add up to $5. Fee sheets get revised, so request the current one before you write a check.

Why does a Butler County deed visit the auditor first?

Ohio makes the deed pass through the auditor's office before the recorder will accept it. As section 319.202 describes it, the buyer files a statement of the property's value, and the auditor writes the fee amount on the deed's face. The recorder's sheet confirms the practice: a conveyance or exemption form and the parcel numbers must travel with every deed.

The recorder's sheet rolls two separate laws into one printed rate:

  • A statewide auditor fee in section 319.54(G)(3) for handling the value statement: one dollar minimum, otherwise ten cents on each $100 or part of $100.
  • An optional county charge under section 322.02, capped at thirty cents on each $100, which the grantor pays to the auditor.
  • The schedule's own wording: $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price, check payable to the Butler County Auditor, plus 50 cents for every parcel number on the deed.

A deed covering several parcels needs the parcel charge repeated, so give the transfer line at 513-887-3154 a call before you file.

Which Butler County deeds are exempt from the transfer charge?

Some deeds are listed in 319.54(G)(3) as free of the auditor's fee. The exemption reason still has to be written on the filing. Situations that come up in family and estate sales include:

  • Spouse to spouse, or parent to child, when the transfer is a gift.
  • A corrective deed that fixes an earlier one.
  • A deed whose only job is securing or releasing a debt.
  • A transfer ordered by a court, apart from a sale made under that order.
  • A conveyance with no payment of any kind that is not a gift either.
  • A pass-through grantee who is not a dealer and buys only to resell promptly.

The law lists many more cases, from government transfers to deeds worth $100 or less. An auditor can tell you which exemption form to attach so the closing agent does not guess.

What gets a deed bounced or billed extra at the Butler County recorder?

The recorder's standardization page applies section 317.114 to papers prepared after June 30, 2009. If a document breaks the layout rules, the office adds $20.00. Court papers, plats, DD214s and state or federal documents are exempt from the layout rules.

  • Type no smaller than 10 point on paper between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Ink in black or blue, with no highlighting anywhere.
  • One inch of white space down each side and along the bottom.
  • Three inches left blank at the top of page one for the recorder, auditor and engineer.
  • A one and a half inch top margin on all following pages.

The fee sheet adds content rules. Each document needs a legal description, affidavits must name the current owner, and papers notarized in Ohio need a prepared by statement. The office refuses blanket assignments and blanket satisfactions, so a lender who paid off several loans must prepare a separate release for each.

Does Butler County take electronic filings or offer fraud alerts?

It does. The recorder's eRecording page names three submission services: Simplifile, CSC and the eRecording Partners Network. A closing office can send a deed through any of them. A separate free service called Property Alert emails a registered user whenever a paper is filed under a chosen name or legal description. That gives an owner of a rental, a vacant house or an inherited house a way to spot a bogus filing early.

The home page also links two fee notices, one for increases effective January 1, 2025 and an older one from 2022 about the reference fee. Treat any printed deed packet that predates them with caution.

What should a Butler County seller know about the county itself?

Butler County stretches across about 470 square miles of southwestern Ohio, mostly in the Great Miami and Little Miami river valleys, with Hamilton County to the south. Wikipedia says it was formed in 1803, names seven cities (Fairfield, Hamilton, Middletown, Monroe, Oxford, Sharonville and Trenton) and notes that Miami University calls the county home. The 2020 count was 390,357 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 400,128. Hamilton is both the seat and the biggest city.

  • Lived in by owners: 69.9 percent of homes in 2020 to 2024.
  • Median owner-occupied value: $258,500.
  • Median household income: $81,590.
  • Homes and apartments counted in mid 2025: 158,143.

The source for these is Census QuickFacts. The Wikipedia page also says the 1913 flood hit Hamilton and Middletown hard, with 46 percent of Hamilton under water, so ask about flood history when a house sits near the Great Miami.

How should an owner approach a quick Butler County sale?

A cash purchase uses the same three stops: deed, auditor, recorder. Whoever runs the closing normally shuttles papers among them. Anyone preparing a deed personally should call the auditor about the transfer charge and the recorder about the page count before signing.

For an inherited house, the signer needs authority from the estate, and the title agent should say which probate documents must be attached. A seller with an old mortgage should also confirm that the lender recorded its release, since an unreleased lien blocks clean title.

What phone number reaches the Butler County recorder?

The fee schedule prints 513-887-3192 and recorder@bcohio.gov. A separate line, 513-887-3154, handles transfer and conveyance questions. Visitors go to 130 High Street in Hamilton.

What is the price of a two-page deed in Butler County?

$39.00 on the schedule effective January 1, 2025, with the $5.00 preservation surcharge built in. Extra pages are $8.00 each. Ask the office for its newest sheet before filing.

Whose name goes on the Butler County transfer fee check?

The Butler County Auditor. The recorder's schedule says so directly and prints the rate as $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price, with 50 cents more per parcel number on a deed.

Can a Butler County deed be filed electronically?

Yes. The recorder's eRecording page lists Simplifile, CSC and the eRecording Partners Network. A closing office can file through any of the three.

Will Butler County accept a deed with no legal description?

No. The schedule says a legal description is required with every document and that deeds also need parcel identification numbers. Without them the filing will not go through.

Where in Springfield does a Clark County deed get filed?

The recorder's office is in the A.B. Graham Building, 31 North Limestone Street, Springfield, OH 45502. The county staff directory lists 937-521-1705 for calls and 937-328-4620 for fax.

The auditor and the treasurer share that address, so one trip can cover the value statement, a tax payoff and the recording. Owners in New Carlisle, the villages and the townships use the same counter. The county's public records page links to a Recorder's Office Title Search and to a Land Records and Property Alerts page, which let you read a recorded deed or lien before you list a house or sign anything.

What does Ohio law charge for recording in Clark County?

Clark County follows the statewide scale in section 317.32. Every charge there is two equal parts, a base fee for the recorder and a housing trust fund fee. A county may also add a preservation surcharge of up to $5 per instrument. The statute says "up to," so ask the office what Clark County charges and request its current sheet.

The statute measures pages at 8.5 by 14 inches and counts the caption page. Going from two pages to three raises the bill.

What happens at the Clark County Auditor before recording?

Under section 319.202, the deed is presented to the auditor ahead of the recorder. The buyer or the buyer's representative files a value statement, electronic or three paper copies, and the auditor endorses the deed with the fee. The auditor's printed address is 31 N. Limestone Street and the phone is 937-521-1860.

  • A statement fee: $1, or ten cents on each $100 (or part of $100) of value, whichever comes out higher, set by section 319.54(G)(3).
  • A transfer tax some counties levy under section 322.02, capped at thirty cents per $100 and adopted only after two public hearings. Ask the auditor whether Clark County has one.
  • The recorder's fees from the table above, paid separately at the counter.

The grantor pays the auditor's fee and any transfer tax, so the seller's closing statement should list them. When the house is residential rental property, the auditor's endorsement also notes that the buyer must file landlord information with the auditor under section 5323.02. A landlord selling a rental should tell the buyer about that duty early, since it falls on the new owner within the closing paperwork.

What tax questions does the Clark County value statement ask?

The value statement doubles as a tax checkpoint. The buyer records either the seller's answer that neither the preceding nor the current year's taxes will be reduced under section 323.152, or a sworn estimate of the reduction when the seller says they will. Homestead and owner-occupancy credits are the usual examples.

A second question concerns land valued for farm use. If the parcel was enrolled, the buyer must acknowledge a possible recoupment charge once it stops qualifying. Clark County's 2020 census count put about a quarter of residents in rural areas, so a seller with acreage should ask the auditor about enrollment before the deed is signed.

Which deeds avoid the Clark County auditor's fee?

Section 319.54(G)(3) excuses a list of transfers, and the filer states the reason in place of paying. A Clark County owner might meet one of these:

  • A deed to or from a federal, state or local government body.
  • A sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A deed that gives or releases debt security.
  • A conveyance valued at $100 or less.
  • A transfer for no payment of money or other tangible value that is not a gift.
  • A lease, unless the term is renewable forever.

The list continues past these. For an exempt deed, the auditor supplies the exemption form that replaces the value statement.

Can you look up Clark County records and set up fraud alerts?

The county's public records page points to a recorder title search and a land records site with property alerts. An alert watches a name or parcel and notifies you when something is filed against it. Owners of rentals, estate houses and empty houses benefit most, since nobody may be home to notice a suspicious filing.

A title company runs the same search before closing. If an old mortgage was paid off but the lender never recorded a release, that release has to be filed first, and recording it carries its own fee.

What is Clark County like for a house seller?

West central Ohio's Clark County covers 403 square miles, the third smallest county in the state by total area. It was created on March 1, 1818 and takes its name from George Rogers Clark. Springfield and New Carlisle are the cities, and Champaign, Madison, Greene, Montgomery and Miami counties surround it. Springfield lies on the Mad River, Buck Creek and Beaver Creek, roughly 45 miles west of Columbus and 25 miles northeast of Dayton. Wittenberg University and Clark State College are both in town. Most city residents attend Springfield City Schools, though parts of the north go to Northeastern Local or Northwestern Local and parts of the west and south to Clark-Shawnee Local.

  • People: 135,340 in July 2025, down 0.5 percent from April 2020.
  • Housing units: 61,550.
  • Owners occupy 69.4 percent of homes (2020 to 2024).
  • Home value at the midpoint for owner-occupied units: $169,900.
  • Monthly rent at the midpoint: $872.

Springfield's economy, Wikipedia says, leaned on factory work for decades and lost thousands of those jobs in the 1990s. Today it relies on healthcare, manufacturing, transportation, leisure, education, finance and retail. Census data counts 2,196 employer establishments in the county in 2023, with 42,831 people employed, and a mean commute of 23.1 minutes.

Those figures come from Census QuickFacts, with geography and school details from the Springfield and Clark County Wikipedia entries.

What should a Clark County owner line up for a rushed sale?

Even a cash closing passes through the auditor and then the recorder. A title agent usually moves the papers, though you can walk them across the hall yourself. For a house that came through an estate, confirm that the person signing has authority from the probate court. Settle liens and back taxes before closing so recording is simple.

Three questions to ask before the signing date: does the county levy a transfer tax, what will the recorder charge for the number of pages in your deed, and does any old mortgage still lack a recorded release?

The A.B. Graham Building, 31 North Limestone Street, Springfield, OH 45502. The county directory lists 937-521-1705 as the office phone.

What does Ohio charge to record the first two pages of a Clark County deed?

State law sets $17 as a base fee plus $17 as a housing trust fund fee, and a county may add up to $5 as a surcharge. Ask the Clark County recorder which surcharge applies and what the current sheet shows.

Does Clark County levy a real property transfer tax?

Ohio lets a county adopt one, capped at thirty cents on every $100 of value, but only the county auditor can say whether Clark County has. The grantor pays it with the auditor's fee.

Are Clark County deeds searchable online?

Yes. The county's public records page links to a Recorder's Office Title Search and a Land Records and Property Alerts page. The alerts notify you of filings under your name or parcel.

Do I go to the auditor or the recorder first with a deed?

The auditor first. Under section 319.202 the buyer's value statement is filed there, and the auditor endorses the deed before it goes to the recorder.

What does the Clermont County recorder do when a house is sold?

The recorder files the deed, the mortgage and the paper that releases the mortgage, then keeps them as the permanent land record for the county. Unlike a car title, a deed is not held by the office or the bank while a loan is outstanding. The original goes back to whoever submitted it, and the recorder keeps the imaged copy.

The office sits at 101 East Main Street, Batavia, Ohio 45103, and takes recordings on weekdays between eight in the morning and four in the afternoon. The main line is 513-732-7236. A title company usually handles this step for both sides of a sale. An owner selling without one can still walk the deed through the three counters in Batavia, and each counter checks something different: the tax map office the legal description, the auditor the fee and the transfer, the recorder the format of the document.

Adding a spouse, removing a former owner or fixing a spelling takes a newly drafted deed, so see an attorney first. In the office's own words, it records what it is handed and does not draft.

How does a deed get recorded in Clermont County?

There are three routes: e-file through an approved partner, mail the packet, or walk it in. E-filing is the fastest, and the office says e-filed documents are typically recorded the same day and show online within 24 hours. Partner companies are listed on the recorder's e-filing page, and fees are paid by ACH.

  • E-file: submissions are processed between 8:30 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. on business days. Anything arriving after that cutoff is worked the following business day, and plats and DD214 discharge papers have to be brought in on paper.
  • Mail: send the prepared document, a check payable to the Clermont County Treasurer, the auditor's conveyance forms, a cover letter naming a contact, plus a return envelope with postage already on it, since the office will not pay to send your document back.
  • In person: a deed starts at the Tax Map Office for a legal description stamp, then goes to the Auditor for the transfer stamp, and only then to the recorder's counter.

The office quotes 1 to 14 days to finish recording, depending on how the packet arrives. Auditor fees need their own check, also made out to the county treasurer, when they travel with the deed.

What does the Clermont County recorder charge?

The recorder's fee schedule prints a basic charge of $34.00 for the first two sides and $8.00 for each added side on 8 1/2 by 14 inch paper. Ohio changed the statewide base fee in October 2024 under Senate Bill 94, and the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer lists $39 for the first two pages. Call 513-732-7236 to confirm which figure applies before writing the check.

A short payment sends the paper back unrecorded. Card payments carry a 2.5% convenience charge with a $2.00 floor.

What does the Clermont County auditor collect before the recorder files a deed?

Transfers pass through the auditor first. The county's published standards set the conveyance fee at $4.00 for each $1,000 of consideration, rounded up to the nearest hundred dollars, and the transfer fee at $0.50 for each parcel. Those standards were adopted under Revised Code 319.203 and took effect January 1, 2024.

Each deed travels with a state conveyance form, DTE 100 for a priced sale or DTE 100EX where the seller claims the fee does not apply. A seller who held the Homestead reduction for the preceding or current tax year adds DTE 101, and a seller with farmland under current agricultural use valuation adds DTE 102. The auditor's office is at the same Batavia address and keeps weekday hours until 4:30 p.m., a half hour past the recorder's closing for new filings.

Why do Clermont County deeds get rejected?

Four problems explain most returned deeds, and each can push a closing back by days.

  • The check is short, or it names the wrong payee.
  • The document has no legal description, or the image is too poor to read.
  • A Social Security number is printed anywhere on the instrument.
  • The deed arrives without the tax map and auditor stamps.

A paper that fails the margin and font rules in Revised Code 317.114 can still be recorded, but the $20 surcharge applies. Plats of condominiums, subdivisions and city lots are the only maps the recorder holds. If the land is acreage with no lot number, the tax map survey sits with the County Engineer, and the auditor's property search shows the same surveys online.

How can I check a Clermont County recording, or protect against deed fraud?

Recorded documents from 1980 forward can be searched on the recorder's website. Printing from the computer at the counter costs 10 cents a page, and pulling a paper book costs $0.25 a page. A copy ordered by mail runs $2.00 a page plus a prepaid return envelope.

The recorder also runs FraudSleuth, a free account that sends an email alert when a document is recorded in a name you enter. You need a separate profile for each spelling, such as first and last, or first, middle initial and last, with no commas or periods. An alert does not prove fraud, since another person may share the name, but it gives an owner a reason to phone 513-732-7236.

The recorder, together with the probate judge and the clerk of the common pleas court, also promotes a Good Deeds Program. Its stated aim is to help owners lower or avoid the cost of probate court, so an heir who inherited a Clermont County house should ask the recorder about it before listing the property.

Once a loan is retired, the lender sends over a release, and the recorder cross-references it to the original mortgage. The county clerk of courts, 513-732-7560, files foreclosure suits, and the sheriff, 513-732-7087, lists auctions.

How big is the Clermont County housing market the recorder serves?

The Census Bureau counts 91,743 housing units for July 1, 2025 and 84,955 households for 2020-2024. Roughly nine in ten residents, 89.3%, had not moved within the prior year. Median monthly owner costs run $1,677 with a mortgage and $646 without. Ask your lender how long it takes to send the release after a payoff, since the recorder indexes that paper only after it arrives.

Property tax is a separate matter from recording and belongs to the treasurer, whose line is 513-732-7254. The recorder will not accept tax payments and refers callers there.

More questions about Clermont County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Which office takes a Clermont County deed for recording?

Record it at the Clermont County Recorder, 101 East Main Street, Batavia, or e-file through an approved partner. In-person deeds first get stamps from the Tax Map Office and the Auditor.

How long does Clermont County take to record a deed?

The office quotes 1 to 14 days depending on the submission method. E-filed documents are typically recorded the same day and appear online within 24 hours.

What is the Clermont County conveyance fee?

The auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of consideration, rounded up to the nearest hundred dollars, plus a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel. These are paid to the auditor, separate from the recorder's check.

Can the recorder write or correct my deed?

No. The office records documents but does not prepare them. Adding or changing a name on a deed needs a new deed drawn up, and the office suggests contacting an attorney.

Does a Clermont County deed need a Homestead statement?

Yes, when the seller was entitled to the Homestead reduction for the preceding or current tax year. DTE 101 goes with the conveyance form.

Columbiana County by the numbers

Who files a deed for a Columbiana County house?

The Columbiana County Recorder files them, at the courthouse in Lisbon. The recorder's website gives 330-424-9517 as the office number. Ohio's section 5301.25 sends every deed to the recorder of the county that holds the land, and it adds a warning: a deed left off the record is treated as fraudulent toward a later purchaser who never heard of it. For a seller, that makes the filing the last step of the sale.

What the office keeps is wider than deeds. Its home page lists mortgages, easements and military discharge papers, and it says new filings are recorded and searchable immediately. Originals come back to whoever submitted them after the staff finish quality control. The same page offers copies of plats and old maps in sizes from 8 by 11 up to 36 by 80, priced from $2 to $5 depending on the paper.

What fees apply when a Columbiana County deed is filed?

The recorder, the auditor and, where it is levied, the county each charge their own rate. The recorder's Documents and Fees page says the state schedule has two equal parts, one for the recorder and one for the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, and that a county may tack on a preservation surcharge of up to $5 whose amount differs from county to county. Phone the office for the Columbiana figure before the closing.

ItemRate stated in the Ohio Revised Code
Deed filing, pages one and two (section 317.32)$17 recorder fee and $17 housing trust fund fee
Every further page (section 317.32)$4 recorder fee and $4 housing trust fund fee

Auditor's conveyance fee (section 319.54)The greater of $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value
Auditor's entry fee (section 319.54)50 cents per transfer
County transfer tax, if levied (section 322.02)No more than 30 cents per $100 of value

Whether the commissioners levy the county transfer tax is a question for the Columbiana County Auditor. The figure above is a ceiling written into the statute, not a promise that it applies here.

Why does the auditor see a Columbiana County deed first?

Because the auditor moves the parcel into the buyer's name on the tax list and endorses the deed before it goes to the recorder. Section 319.202 has the buyer file a value statement, and it makes the seller pay the conveyance fee. Value here includes any mortgage balance that stays on the property.

The form asks two things that suit this county's mix of town lots and farms. One is whether the property carried an owner-occupancy or homestead tax reduction. The other is whether the land was enrolled in the agricultural use valuation program, and what happens to the recoupment charge if it leaves. Sellers of acreage in the northern townships should expect that second question.

The statute also lists transfers that owe no conveyance fee. Examples include:

  • Gifts within a marriage or from parent to child
  • Splits between heirs when nobody pays money
  • Corrective deeds that fix an earlier one
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust by its maker

The reason for any exemption goes on the value statement, so write it down before you visit the auditor in Lisbon.

What must a deed show before the auditor accepts it?

Section 5301.01 requires the seller's signature, acknowledged before a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer, notary or mayor. A notary at your bank or title company covers that. Under section 319.20 the auditor also wants these in hand:

  • A mailing address for at least one buyer
  • The volume and page, or other marker, of the seller's own deed
  • A legal description that lines up with the tax list

When only part of a parcel changes hands, the auditor divides the tax value between the piece sold and the piece kept. Any back taxes on the original parcel are then shared out by value if the buyer or the remaining owner asks.

Where is Columbiana County and what shaped its housing?

The county lies on Ohio's eastern edge. Pennsylvania is on its east side, Mahoning County on the north, and about 20 miles of Ohio River frontage on the south. The county's own history page counts 534 square miles and 18 townships. The glacier's southern limit crosses the county near Lisbon, so the north is level, fertile farmland and the south is hilly, with limestone soils better for pasture, orchards and timber.

Settlement came early. Cabins went up in St. Clair Township around 1792 or 1793, and the legislature organized the county on March 25, 1803, the same year a Baptist minister platted Lisbon as New Lisbon. The word New was dropped in 1895. Towns followed the river, the Sandy and Beaver Canal and then the railroads: Wellsville in 1797, East Liverpool in 1798 and Salem in 1806. East Liverpool became a pottery center after 1839, and Salem later built pumps and auto bodies.

By the 2020 census Salem was the largest city at 11,915 people, then East Liverpool at 9,958 and Columbiana at 6,559. Lisbon counted 2,597 and East Palestine 4,761. East Palestine is also where a freight train derailed on February 3, 2023 and is part of the county's recent history.

What do the Census figures say about Columbiana County homes?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for the county lists the following:

  • 99,377 residents at the July 1, 2025 estimate, 2.5% below the April 2020 estimate base
  • 46,220 housing units and 41,459 households
  • 72.7% of homes owner-occupied
  • Median home value of $151,600 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median rent of $756 a month
  • Median household income of $58,180
  • 58 building permits in 2025

Those are countywide medians. A house on a village street in Lisbon and a farmhouse in Madison Township will sit far apart, so use a written offer or local appraisal for the real number on your own property.

What can a seller line up before heading to Lisbon?

Most of this is a phone call each:

  • Ask the county treasurer what is owed on the parcel so the title company can clear it from the proceeds
  • Ask any lender to record a release of an old mortgage
  • If the owner has died, ask the probate court which papers allow a sale and who signs
  • Match the legal description on your deed to the tax record
  • Agree on who covers any farm-use recoupment or open assessment

The same route applies when a house is sold as-is for cash. The deed still passes through the auditor first and the recorder second, in the same order. Salem, East Liverpool, Columbiana and the villages all file in the same Lisbon office, so a seller in Wellsville or Leetonia does not need a separate local filing. Bring the signed deed, the completed value statement and a way to pay each office, and ask at the counter how the recorder and the auditor want the payments handed in.

More questions about Columbiana County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Can I reach the Columbiana County Recorder by phone?

Yes. The recorder's website gives 330-424-9517 for the office, which is based at the courthouse in Lisbon.

What is the preservation surcharge on a deed filed in Columbiana County?

State law lets a county charge up to $5 per document, and the recorder's site says the amount varies by county. Ask the office for the current Columbiana County charge.

Does the buyer or the seller pay the conveyance fee?

The seller pays it under section 319.202, while the buyer files the statement of value. If the county levies a transfer tax, the seller pays that as well.

Can relatives transfer a house without the conveyance fee?

Often, yes. Section 319.54 exempts gifts between spouses or between a parent and child, and splits among heirs when no money is paid. The reason must be stated on the value statement.

What if the deed is signed but never filed?

The deed is still a signed document, but section 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later purchaser with no knowledge of it. Filing with the recorder closes that gap.

Where does a Crawford County deed get recorded?

The office follows sections 317.11 and 317.112 of the Ohio Revised Code, which set what a document must look like before staff accept it.

One local rule surprises people. According to the recorder's FAQ, a document that transfers real estate has to be approved first, and that process starts at the Crawford County Engineer's office, not at the recorder. The recorder also points out that its staff cannot give legal advice, so it suggests an attorney or title agency prepare the deed. Fill-in-the-blank forms exist, but the office stresses that the person submitting them is responsible for meeting every legal requirement.

What fees does the Bucyrus recorder print for a deed?

The recorder's fee page announces a $5 increase that took effect January 1, 2025 under Senate Bill 94, bringing the standard recording fee to $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that. The office notes that each printed side counts as one page, and that $4 reference fees and the office's standardization guidelines still apply. The page-by-page figures it prints are:

A few other items on the same schedule can come up in a sale. A release of a lien costs $4, a federal tax lien filing costs $5, and a document carrying a marginal notation adds $4 per notation to the regular fee. Plats and condominium drawings are priced by area, at $0.10 per square inch with a $40 minimum per page. The checklist asks filers to bring separate checks for the recorder, the auditor and the treasurer.

What does the Crawford County Recorder want to see on a deed?

The recorder publishes an eleven-point guide, and these are the points that trip up sellers most often:

  • The document must be an original, signed and notarized
  • A deed prepared in Ohio must carry a prepared-by statement
  • It must include the complete legal description, which the office uses for geographic indexing
  • Later documents should cite the book and page of earlier recordings
  • Exhibits and schedules must be clearly identified
  • The preparer's name and address, a return address and a phone number for minor fixes should appear
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope gets the original back without postage charges

The office adds that it is the filer's job to make sure pages are legible enough to scan. The checklist ends with a reminder to review the work, especially the fees, to avoid rejection.

When it indexes a deed, the office searches by legal description rather than street address. If you only have the house number, the recorder's FAQ says to find the owner name and transfer date through the Crawford County Auditor's search page first.

What does the Crawford County Auditor add to a sale?

The auditor sets the value that tax bills rest on and receives the conveyance paperwork. Its real estate page says property is revalued every three years under Ohio Department of Taxation rules, that taxes are figured on 35% of market value, and that Crawford County has 54 taxing districts, each with its own rate. No owner pays more than 10 mills of unvoted levies, and the voted portion depends on local elections.

Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement and the seller pays the conveyance fee, plus any county transfer tax that the commissioners have levied under section 322.02. The statutory conveyance fee is $1 or 10 cents per $100, whichever is greater, according to section 319.54. Ask the Crawford County Auditor which county rate applies, since the statute only caps it at 30 cents per $100.

The auditor's page also describes several items that matter to a seller:

  • Owners may contest a value from January 1 to March 31 before the Board of Revision
  • New construction or an improvement over $2,000 must be reported, and failure can bring a 50% penalty on the owner's taxes
  • Building permits are issued by the cities of Bucyrus and Galion, Jackson, Jefferson and Polk townships, and the villages of Crestline, New Washington, North Robinson and Chatfield
  • Farmland in the current agricultural use value program pays a one-time $25 enrollment fee
  • Manufactured home buyers have 30 days to register with the auditor, or face a $100 penalty

What is Crawford County like for a home seller?

Crawford County sits in north central Ohio. Wikipedia lists it as the fourth smallest county in the state by total area, at 403 square miles, with the Sandusky and Olentangy rivers draining it. Bucyrus is the county seat and largest city, and Galion is the other city. The county is named for Colonel William Crawford, and it makes up the Bucyrus micropolitan area. Neighbors are Seneca, Huron, Richland, Morrow, Marion and Wyandot counties.

The county's population peaked at 50,364 in 1970 and counted 42,025 in 2020, with the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate at 41,896. Public libraries in Bucyrus, Galion and Crestline serve the county. In the 2020 census, 65.9% of residents lived in urban areas and 34.1% in rural areas, a split that explains why a Bucyrus lot and a township farmhouse can be priced so differently.

How do Crawford County homes compare on the numbers?

QuickFacts, the Census Bureau's county profile, prints these figures for Crawford:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $136,700 in the 2020 to 2024 survey
  • Owner-occupied rate: 73.1%
  • Housing units: 19,813, with 18,059 households
  • Median gross rent: $794
  • Median household income: $58,044, with 11.2% of people in poverty
  • Building permits in 2025: 3
  • Median owner cost with a mortgage: $1,081 a month, and $487 without one

Only three building permits were counted for 2025, so housing here is mostly what already stands. A written cash offer or a local appraisal can price a particular house more reliably than a countywide median can. Sellers in Galion, Crestline, Bucyrus and the townships all record in the same Bucyrus office.

What should be settled before heading to Bucyrus?

The recorder's FAQ makes clear that it does not release liens. It records them, and the Treasurer or the Clerk of Courts handles the underlying tax and court filings. That means a seller should sort out the following with the right office before the deed is filed:

  • Ask the County Treasurer for the unpaid tax figure so the title company can pay it from the proceeds
  • Ask a lender to file a release of any old mortgage, since the recorder only records it
  • Check with the Clerk of Courts for judgments tied to the owner
  • Ask the County Engineer's office about the transfer approval step
  • Match the legal description to the one on your last deed

The same steps apply when the buyer is paying cash and the house is sold as-is.

The office number printed on the recorder's website is 419-562-6961. The office is in Bucyrus.

How much does it cost to record a three-page deed in Crawford County?

The recorder's fee table prints $47.00 for three pages. That is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for the third, before any other charges the document triggers.

Does the recorder remove liens from my title?

No. The office only records certain liens and says it does not remove or release them. Property tax liens go through the County Treasurer, and court matters through the Clerk of Courts.

Where does the transfer process start in Crawford County?

At the County Engineer's office, according to the recorder's FAQ. A document that transfers real estate has to be approved there before it moves on.

Can I search records by street address at the recorder?

Not directly. The recorder indexes by legal description, so look up the owner name or transfer date on the County Auditor's search page if you only have an address.

Where is the Fairfield County Recorder, and what does the office keep?

The Fairfield County Recorder works from the Administrative Courthouse at 210 East Main Street, Suite 205, in Lancaster, and keeps weekday hours of 8:00 am to 4:00 pm. The phone number is 740-652-7100. The office keeps the permanent public record of deeds, mortgages, leases, liens, plats, powers of attorney and military discharges for the county.

Indexes reach back to 1800, and scanned documents are searchable online from January 1980 forward. Staff will help you find the right desk, but they do not run searches for you, help draft a document, or hand out recording forms. A deed has to be written by someone else, such as a closing agent or an attorney.

What must happen before a Fairfield County deed reaches the Recorder?

The deed goes to the County Auditor first, and only after the Auditor completes the transfer does it go to the Recorder. A Fairfield County sale usually needs two papers at the Auditor: the deed itself and a conveyance fee statement, which is Ohio form DTE 100 (or DTE 100EX when an exemption applies).

The Auditor's Map Room checks the legal description against the county conveyance standards before it accepts the deed. A prepared deed can be emailed to the Map Room for that approval, and the approval is a pre-requisite for the transfer. After approval, the deed and statement can be dropped at the transfer desk at 108 N. High Street in Lancaster, or mailed to the Auditor marked Attn: Conveyance.

Under Ohio law the buyer or the buyer's representative files the statement of value, and the seller pays the conveyance fee. The statement defines value as the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage included. For a gift, value is the estimated open market price. Writing a false value on purpose is prohibited by the statute (R.C. 319.202).

What will a Fairfield County deed transfer and recording run?

Two separate bills apply: the Auditor's transfer and conveyance charges, and the Recorder's page-based recording fee. The table lists the rates exactly as the official pages print them.

ChargeRate as publishedPaid to

The Recorder's own fee schedule is linked from the Recorder page, so confirm the surcharge and any other line there before you write a check. A county can also levy a real property transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02, which the grantor pays to the Auditor before the Recorder sees the deed.

Who can acknowledge a deed in Ohio, and where must it be recorded?

An Ohio deed must be signed by the grantor, and the signing must be acknowledged before an authorized officer (R.C. 5301.01). The statute names these officers:

  • a judge or clerk of a court of record in Ohio
  • a county auditor or county engineer
  • a notary public
  • a mayor

A deed is filed where the land sits. Under R.C. 5301.25, a deed that has not been recorded is treated as fraudulent against a later good faith buyer who had no knowledge of it. For a Fairfield County house, that means the deed belongs on file in Lancaster, whether the home sits in Pickerington, Canal Winchester, Reynoldsburg or an unincorporated township.

The Recorder enters each instrument in the order presented, with the date and exact time. Ohio law (R.C. 317.13) lets the Recorder decline an instrument that is materially false or fraudulent, and a person whose instrument is refused can ask the Court of Common Pleas to order recording.

Can a Fairfield County deed be recorded electronically?

Yes, through Simplifile, which the Auditor's fact sheet names as the electronic filing route. The Auditor adds that a one-time filer may find the process impractical and can use paper instead.

Ohio set a statutory target of June 30, 2026 for every county recorder, auditor and engineer to offer electronic recording of real property conveyances, and for recorders to post electronic indexes and images of instruments recorded since January 1, 1980. That date has passed, and it lines up with the 1980 online start on the Fairfield page. A recorder may require a username and password to view those records but cannot charge for one.

Paper filing still works. Mail or drop off the deed with the Auditor, then send the Recorder its fee. Ask the Recorder's office at 740-652-7100 how to get the original returned to you.

What should a Fairfield County seller know about the county itself?

Fairfield County was founded December 9, 1800, with Lancaster as county seat and largest city. It covers 509 square miles, mostly land, and had 158,921 residents at the 2020 census. The county belongs to the Columbus metropolitan area. Franklin County lies to the northwest, Licking County to the north, Perry County to the east, Hocking County to the south and Pickaway County to the southwest, so a mailing address in a neighboring county does not change where a Fairfield County parcel is recorded.

The northern part is flat and was glaciated, while the land south of U.S. 22 turns hilly toward the Hocking Hills. Buckeye Lake lies partly in the northeast corner. Cities named on the county page include Lancaster, Pickerington, Canal Winchester and Reynoldsburg. Ask the city or township office where the house sits about any open permit before you list.

Because the Auditor, Recorder and Treasurer sit in separate offices, build a short checklist before closing: legal description approved, conveyance fee statement signed, taxes confirmed with the Treasurer, then recording.

  • Legal description cleared by the Auditor's Map Room
  • Deed signed and acknowledged before an authorized officer
  • Statement of value (DTE 100 or DTE 100EX) completed
  • Transfer and conveyance fees paid at the Auditor's transfer desk
  • Recording fee sent to the Recorder

What should I do if I suspect fraud on a Fairfield County property?

Enroll in the Recorder's free alerts first, since they flag new documents filed under your name or a notary's name. Then call the Recorder at 740-652-7100 to ask what was filed, and contact an attorney about next steps.

The Recorder also issues Veteran ID cards, and the office asks callers to phone 740-652-7100 for that service.

More questions about Fairfield County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Which office files a deed for a Fairfield County house?

At the Fairfield County Recorder, 210 East Main Street, Suite 205, Lancaster, after the County Auditor has processed the transfer. The Auditor's office is a separate stop at 108 N. High Street.

What does the Auditor charge to transfer a deed in Fairfield County?

The Auditor's fact sheet lists a $.50 per parcel transfer fee and a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of consideration when money changes hands. Ask the transfer desk to confirm the amount before you bring payment.

Does Fairfield County have its own deed form?

No. The Recorder does not provide forms for recording and staff cannot help prepare a document. A title company or attorney usually drafts the deed, and the Auditor's Map Room reviews the legal description.

Can I look up old Fairfield County deeds from home?

Yes. Indexes go back to 1800 and images are online from January 1980 forward through the Recorder's land records search. Older documents are at the office.

Who pays the conveyance fee when a house sells?

The seller does. Ohio law puts the conveyance fee on the grantor, while the buyer files the statement of value with the Auditor.

Where is the Fayette County Recorder, and what does the office handle?

The county page lists the kinds of papers the office files:

  • deeds, mortgages and land contracts
  • IRS liens and mechanics liens
  • plats and zoning resolutions
  • military service discharges

Washington Court House is the county seat and the county's only city. Every deed for a Fayette County parcel is recorded at this one office, whether the house is in town or out in a township.

Ohio Revised Code 317.32 sets the structure behind these numbers: a base fee and a housing trust fund fee for each page, plus an optional document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars that the county may keep for its general fund.

How do I deliver a deed to the Fayette County Recorder?

Bring it to Suite 305 or mail it, and pay by cash or check. The Recorder states that credit and debit cards are not accepted.

  • Documents received after 3:30 PM are held and run the next day, so a late afternoon drop does not get that day's time stamp.
  • Anything that must be mailed back needs a self-addressed, stamped envelope included with the papers.
  • Since June 22, 2026, the county offers e-recording through Simplifile for both conveyance and non-conveyance documents.

The time stamp matters because Ohio recorders file instruments in order of presentation and note the exact time (R.C. 317.13). If two papers arrive for the same house, the earlier time gets priority.
