The Auditor's real estate department tracks deed transfers, new parcels, lot splits and homestead exemptions, and a deed for a sale is presented there before it goes to the Recorder. The Auditor's office is at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 303, with the phone at 740-335-6461 and the same Monday to Friday, 8 am to 4 pm schedule.

The Auditor's forms page carries the conveyance papers: the Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100), the Exemption from Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100EX), a statement for homestead property, a statement for current agricultural use valuation property, and forms for mobile homes. The county also posts its conveyance standards for legal descriptions.

The DTE 100 asks for the total consideration and then the portion paid for items other than real property, and the fee is figured on the real property consideration that remains. It also asks whether the seller said the home receives the senior or disabled homestead exemption or farm use valuation, and whether the buyer will live there by January 1 of the next year. The form itself warns that skipping the owner-occupancy application blocks that 2.5 percent reduction until a proper, timely application is filed, so fill that part in. Ask the Auditor for the county's current conveyance fee rate before closing.

Which papers can a Fayette County Recorder refuse to record?

An Ohio recorder may decline an instrument that is not required or authorized to be recorded, or that the recorder has reasonable cause to believe is materially false or fraudulent. Someone whose paper is turned away can ask the Court of Common Pleas to order recording.

One refusal is mandatory. The recorder must refuse a right-to-list home sale agreement described in R.C. 5301.94. A Fayette County owner who is told such an agreement will be recorded against the house should know the statute directs the recorder to turn it away.

A recorder has no duty to inspect or investigate what is handed over. Checking the legal description, names and signatures is the job of whoever drafted the deed.

What do copies and small extras cost under Ohio law?

R.C. 317.32 sets several charges besides the recording fee, each split into a base fee and a housing trust fund fee of equal size:

  • Certified copy of a recorded document: $1 base plus $1 trust fund per page, with a further 50 cents plus 50 cents when the recorder's seal is required.
  • Photocopy outside the recording process: $1 plus $1 per page.
  • Marginal reference entered by a separate instrument: $2 plus $2 for each reference, which matches the $4.00 marginal fee Fayette posts.
  • Local fax or electronic transmission: $1 plus $1 per page.

For a seller, a certified copy of the vesting deed is the most common extra, and a title company often asks for one.

How do Fayette County values and tax bills connect to a sale?

The Auditor is the county's chief fiscal officer and also its real property appraiser. Ohio directs a general reappraisal every six years, with an update in the third year. Each year the Auditor prepares the tax list, and after the Treasurer collects, the Auditor distributes the money to townships, schools and other taxing bodies. The Auditor also certifies and publishes the list of delinquent taxes, and the Treasurer then pursues those accounts.

The Auditor serves as secretary of the county Board of Revision, and the Board of Revision Property Complaint form is on the Auditor's forms page. A seller who disputes a value uses that form, and does not take the question to the Recorder.

At the deed stage, state law requires the conveyance statement to confirm that the seller was asked whether the home gets a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, and whether it was in farm use valuation. If farm use ends, a recoupment charge can follow, and buyer and seller are expected to account for it between themselves (R.C. 319.202). A seller of acreage that has been in farm use should raise this with the title agent early.

What should a seller know about Fayette County?

Fayette County was formed on March 1, 1810 from parts of Highland and Ross counties and named for the Marquis de Lafayette. It covers 407 square miles of nearly all land and counted 28,951 residents in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 28,552. The median age was 41.5 years, and 19.2 percent of residents were 65 or older.

The county touches Madison, Pickaway, Ross, Highland, Clinton and Greene counties. Washington Court House anchors a micropolitan area that is part of the Columbus-Marion-Zanesville region. Good Hope and Pancoastburg are the named unincorporated places on the county map. The Tri-County Triangle Trail connects Washington Court House with Chillicothe.

If the Auditor's online data for your parcel looks wrong, the Auditor's page asks owners to report the problem so the record can be corrected.

$39.00, according to the Recorder's printed schedule, and the $4.00 marginal fee can apply on top. A one page deed is also $39.00, and three pages cost $47.00.

Can I pay the Fayette County Recorder by card?

No. The Recorder accepts cash or check only, and credit and debit cards are not accepted.

Can I e-record a deed in Fayette County?

Yes. As of June 22, 2026, the county offers e-recording through Simplifile for conveyance and non-conveyance documents. Paper filing at Suite 305 remains available.

What time should I get a deed to the Fayette County Recorder?

Before 3:30 PM. Documents received after that hour are held and run the following day.

Does the Fayette County Recorder or Auditor handle the conveyance form?

The Auditor, at Suite 303 of the same building. The Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100) and the exemption form (DTE 100EX) are on the Auditor's forms page, and the Recorder then files the deed.

What is the order of steps to record a deed in Franklin County?

  • Prepare a new deed form. A template is available through the County Law Library under real estate forms.
  • Get the legal description from the last deed on file, which the Recorder's website lets you search, and follow the county document standards.

  • Include a separate payment for the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards the deed to the Recorder once the transfer is complete.

Paying off a mortgage does not call for a new deed. The lender files a release of mortgage as its own document.

When the seller is receiving the homestead exemption at the time of transfer, the county's $2 piece is waived and the conveyance fee drops to $1 per $1,000. You can verify homestead status on the Auditor's property search under the Homestead Credit entry on the parcel summary. Round the sale amount up to the next $100 when you use the calculator.

  • A self-addressed, stamped envelope for the original

The Recorder's fee calculator and the Auditor's transfer calculator both help you total these amounts before you leave home.

Franklin County was created April 30, 1803, less than two months after Ohio became a state, and was named for Benjamin Franklin. It covers about 544 square miles and had 1,323,807 residents in 2020, which makes it the most populous county in Ohio. Columbus is the county seat and the state capital.

Suburbs on the county list include Bexley, Dublin, Gahanna, Grandview Heights, Grove City, Hilliard, New Albany, Upper Arlington, Westerville and Worthington. The 2020 census found 540,369 households here and a median age of 34.2 years. Whatever the size of the market, each sale goes through the same paperwork, so a complete packet saves a second trip.

The Auditor first. After the transfer is complete, the deed goes to the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards it if you included a separate payment for the Recorder.

  • Auditor: Suite 165 in the same building, the first stop. Its real estate line is (419) 337-9200.
  • Land records search: reached from the county's Records Search page, for looking up earlier deeds and mortgages.

The Recorder page also carries a Real Property Conveyance Standards PDF plus printable plats and land surveys. Read them before you draft a legal description.

What steps come before a Fulton County deed reaches the Recorder?

Fulton County's conveyance standards exist to give every legal description a uniform check, correct visible errors and describe the parcel properly for tax purposes. Odd cases go to a panel of the County Engineer, the Auditor and the Planning Director.

  1. Write the deed so its legal description follows the last deed of record.
  2. Sign before a notary. Under R.C. 5301.01 a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer or mayor can also take the acknowledgment.
  3. Take the deed to Suite 165 for the description check, the conveyance fee and the transfer.
  4. Carry it to Suite 175 and pay the recording fee.

Ohio's transfer tax statute has the grantor settle with the Auditor before the deed is handed to the Recorder, so keep this order. Ask the Recorder which endorsement it expects to see.

What does the Fulton County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

The Auditor's price list reads $4.00 per thousand dollars of total consideration, rounded up to the nearest $100, and $0.50 per parcel as a transfer fee. Its own worked example treats $100,001 as $100,100 and arrives at $400.40.

State law builds that number in layers. R.C. 319.54(G)(3) sets a statement-of-value fee of ten cents per $100, and R.C. 322.02 lets a county add as much as thirty cents per $100. The grantor pays on delivery of the deed.

Some transfers carry no fee at all under R.C. 319.54(G)(3), including:

  • gifts between spouses, or from a parent to a child;
  • a transfer where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and the deal is no gift;
  • conveyances among the heirs or devisees of one decedent for no money;
  • a trustee handing property back to the grantor of a revocable trust.

If your sale resembles one of these, ask the Auditor's real estate office before you assume a fee is due.

What will recording a Fulton County deed cost?

The state sets the recording fees, and half of each goes to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. Every printed side counts as a page. Counties may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at $5.00 per document, so phone the Fulton Recorder for the final figure before mailing a check.

What formatting rules does Fulton County enforce on a deed?

R.C. 317.114 sets a standard layout for any deed you hand the Recorder. A deed that misses it is still taken but carries an added $10 base fee and $10 housing trust fee.

  • Type no smaller than ten point.
  • Sheets no smaller than letter size and no longer than 14 inches.
  • Ink in black or blue, nothing highlighted.
  • One inch of white space down both sides and along the foot of each page.
  • Three inches of white space across the head of page one, which the Engineer, Auditor and Recorder use for their endorsements, and one and a half inches on following pages.

The rule skips court and tax-authority papers, plats, state and federal documents, and anything signed before July 1, 2009.

How big and how stable is the Fulton County housing market?

The Census Bureau recorded 42,713 residents in April 2020 and put the July 2025 estimate at 41,853, down 2.0 percent. Owners occupy 80.2 percent of the housing, the median owner-occupied unit is worth $191,000, and the county gave out 57 building permits during 2025. Median household income stands at $72,864.

The county spreads across 405 square miles of land at roughly 105 residents per square mile. Parcels range from farm acreage to village lots in Archbold and Wauseon to homes in any of its twelve townships, Amboy and Chesterfield through Swan Creek and York.

What else shows up in Fulton County's land records during a sale?

A title search in Wauseon covers more than the last deed. The Sheriff's Office explains in its own FAQ that when a house is sold at a sheriff's sale, liens are paid in order from the proceeds and then cancelled against the property, except a federal lien, which stays on file at the Recorder. Buyers at those sales are told to check every lien themselves.

  • Mortgages, releases and assignments are filed in the same office as the deed.
  • Federal tax liens are filed with the Recorder at a $5.00 fee, and releases cost $3.00.
  • Military discharge papers are recorded without a charge.
  • Plats and condominium drawings are priced at ten cents per square inch with a $40.00 minimum.

Search the parcel in the Recorder's land records and the Auditor's property search before you agree on a closing date.

Which Fulton County tax rules should a home seller check?

Fulton County real estate tax bills fall due in February and July. According to the Auditor, the lien date is January 1 and Ohio taxes run one year in arrears: the bill paid in 2025 was for tax year 2024 and was figured on what the home was worth when 2025 began.

  • Owner-occupied reduction: residences only, and it is never applied on its own. Call (419) 337-9200 to enroll.
  • Value complaints: go to the Board of Revision in the window from the first of January to the last day of March.
  • Payments and tax-mailing address changes: the Treasurer handles both, not the Auditor.

Request a payoff figure for the parcel from the Fulton County Treasurer, and have the title company explain who covers each bill.

More questions about Fulton County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Is there a transfer tax collected by the Fulton County Recorder?

The Recorder takes the recording fee only. The conveyance fee of $4.00 per $1,000 and the $0.50 per parcel transfer fee belong to the Auditor, and Ohio law has the grantor pay the Auditor ahead of the filing.

Can a Fulton County deed skip the Auditor and go straight to recording?

Plan on visiting the Auditor first. R.C. 322.02 has the grantor pay the county Auditor before the deed is presented to the Recorder, and the county's conveyance standards put each legal description through a check.

What hours does the Wauseon Recorder keep?

Weekdays, half past eight to half past four, at Suite 175, 152 S. Fulton St. The phone is (419) 337-9232. The Auditor is in Suite 165 of the same building.

What happens if my deed has a small font or thin margins?

The Recorder still files it, but under R.C. 317.114 the bill rises by $10 in base fee and $10 in housing trust fee. Court papers, plats, state and federal documents and instruments signed before July 1, 2009 are excluded.

Where do I send a complaint that my Fulton County home is overvalued?

Address it to the Board of Revision through the Auditor's real estate office at (419) 337-9200. The filing window runs from January 1 to March 31, and the Auditor's staff can mail a form or point you to the printable copy.

Who records deeds in Gallia County, Ohio?

Gallia County dates to March 25, 1803, and runs along the Ohio River where Ohio meets West Virginia. French settlers gave it the name, and Welsh families arrived in 1818. Gallipolis is the seat, with Cheshire, Crown City, Rio Grande, Centerville and Vinton as the other villages, and every one of them files into the same land records. Part of the Wayne National Forest sits inside the county line.

Where is the Gallia County Recorder's office and what are its hours?

The Recorder is at 18 Locust Street, Gallipolis, Ohio 45631. Weekday hours run eight to four. Call 740-446-4612 and ask for extension 1247, 1248 or 1329.

  • County Auditor: same address, Room 1264, with the real estate desk on extension 1201.

What comes first in Gallia County: the Auditor or the Recorder?

The Auditor comes first. The Recorder's requirements for deeds say plainly that a deed must be transferred in the Auditor's office before it is recorded.

On its website the Auditor posts a conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator under Tools, with the statement of value form for the conveyance fee among its forms. The statewide piece of the conveyance fee is a dollar, or ten cents per hundred dollars of value if that is larger (R.C. 319.54(G)(3)). A county board may stack a tax of up to thirty cents per hundred on top (R.C. 322.02). Use the Auditor's calculator for Gallia County's total, and ask the real estate desk about exemptions such as a transfer with no money or other consideration.

The Auditor's office also reports that Gallia County has more than 29,000 parcels and more than 2,500 manufactured and mobile homes, and its website announces a Community Reinvestment Area that began on December 2, 2024. Ask the Auditor what that program covers for your parcel.

What does the Gallia County Recorder require on a deed?

The Recorder publishes a checklist, and a deed or mortgage that misses an item comes back. The list includes:

  • a full legal description naming the township or city, lot or subdivision and acreage;
  • grantor names spelled exactly as they are signed and notarized;
  • the permanent parcel number wherever the real estate is described;
  • a notary signature, seal and expiration date;
  • a "prepared by" line, which Ohio requires;
  • names typed beneath the original signatures;
  • a stamped, addressed return envelope big enough to hold the papers.

The office also warns that its deputies cannot fix a lot number or other typo. Whoever made the document must make the change. Documents boxed for pickup must be claimed within a week or they are mailed out at the box holder's cost.

How much does the Gallia County Recorder charge?

Leave an inch of white space on the sides and the bottom, three inches at the head of the first page and an inch and a half at the head of later ones.

Marginal clutter such as page numbers, initials and bar codes is not charged.

Which other Gallia County records show up in a sale?

Title work on a Gallia County house often turns up more than the deed. The Recorder's fee page lists the other filings that sit in the same indexes.

  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement.
  • Federal tax liens and releases, personal property tax liens and workers' compensation liens.
  • Land contracts, powers of attorney and trust documents.
  • A Notice to Medicaid Estate Recovery of Pending Transfer of Property, a form the Recorder links on its fees page.

Run the parcel through the Recorder's search and the Auditor's search before you sign a contract. A lien found after a contract is signed holds up the closing.

What does Census data say about Gallia County housing?

The 2020 count for Gallia was 29,220 people, and the July 2025 estimate is 29,072. Three of every four homes are owner-held (74.7 percent), their median value is $155,600, and the county's median rent is $813 against a median household income of $56,830.

Gallia's land area is about 467 square miles, and the 2020 Census found 13.1 percent of the 13,430 housing units vacant. Only seven building permits were issued in 2025. A seller here is often handling an older house in a county where new construction is thin, which makes the title and lien check even more worth doing.

Gallipolis is the county seat and largest village, and the county is part of the Point Pleasant, West Virginia and Ohio micropolitan area, with Cabell and Mason counties across the river. Bring that in when you talk to a buyer from across the state line: the deed still records in Gallipolis, and the Auditor's records and the Recorder's records are the two places to check first.

The Recorder's fee page lists $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after them. The state base is $34, which a county may raise with a preservation surcharge of up to $5.

Which Gallipolis office comes first, the Auditor or the Recorder?

Yes. Per the Recorder's own deed requirements, the transfer in the Auditor's office has to happen before recording. Both offices are at 18 Locust Street, and the Auditor's real estate desk is on extension 1201.

Can the Recorder correct an error in my legal description?

No. The office says deputies cannot change lot numbers or other details even when the error looks like a typo. The person who prepared the document has to fix it and sign again.

How does a deed get recorded in Geauga County?

A Geauga County deed passes through three offices in Chardon, and the county publishes a one-page reference sheet effective June 30, 2026 that lays out the order. First the Engineer approves the legal description. Next the Auditor transfers the parcel and takes the conveyance fee. Last, the Recorder files the deed and sends it back.

Geauga sits in Ohio's northeast corner inside the Cleveland metropolitan area, with Chardon as its seat. The county was founded on March 1, 1806, as the second county in the Connecticut Western Reserve, and its first settlement was at Burton in 1798.

What does each of the three Chardon offices handle?

The reference sheet lists the three stops, their addresses and what each one needs from you.

  • County Engineer, 12665 Merritt Rd, Chardon, phone (440) 279-1800: reviews the legal description and stamps it with an original (wet) stamp. No fee. Allow 2 to 3 business days. Bring a legible copy of the prior deed with its volume and page reference.
  • County Auditor, 231 Main St, Suite 1-A, phone (440) 279-1600: transfers the property and updates the tax records. Needs the original signed and notarized deed.
  • County Recorder, 231 Main St, Suite 1-C, phone (440) 279-2020: records the deed and mails the original back.

The Recorder's page puts the Auditor two doors down the hall. To send a deed by mail, enclose a brief letter saying what you want done, your phone number, a stamped return envelope and two separate checks, payable to the Recorder and to the Auditor.

What does the Geauga County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

The Auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value and $0.50 per parcel, and checks for both are made payable to the Geauga County Auditor. The Recorder's FAQ also puts the conveyance fee at four dollars per thousand and refers fee questions to the Auditor.

Ohio law explains the split. The first layer is the statement-of-value fee in R.C. 319.54(G)(3), ten cents on each hundred dollars. The second is a county tax capped at thirty cents per hundred under R.C. 322.02, which the grantor pays to the Auditor ahead of recording. The statute exempts some transfers, among them spousal and parent-to-child gifts, deals with no consideration and certain trust moves.

The Recorder asks for a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX conveyance form with the deed. A Transfer on Death Affidavit is the exception the Recorder names: it has no Auditor fee.

How much does the Geauga County Recorder charge?

State law fixes the Recorder's charge at $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page that follows. A check that is short or too large gets the document returned unrecorded, so count pages before writing it.

The reference sheet says electronic recording of conveyances is available and lets you skip the paper steps, and the 2026 sheet also says legal descriptions presented that way do not need the wet Engineer stamp. An older Recorder page still says eRecording is not available for any document that needs conveyance through the Auditor, so call (440) 279-2020 to confirm what the office will take.

Paper filings are on a fast clock. The Recorder's FAQ gives same-day turnaround, and an electronic recording is returned when it is recorded. Leave a self-addressed stamped envelope with an in-person deed, or come back the next day to pick it up.

The sheet lists what each deed needs before it reaches the counter.

  • Legible signatures, and printed names under any that are hard to read.
  • A line naming whoever prepared the deed.

  • The 8-digit permanent parcel numbers.

The extra $20 for a non-standard document comes from R.C. 317.114, which wants at least ten point type, black or blue ink and three blank inches above the text on page one. Staff cannot notarize or give legal advice, and state law keeps them from running title searches. The Recorder stopped accepting Torrens registered land filings, and it does not sell blank forms.

What else does the Geauga County Recorder keep for owners and sellers?

The Recorder's FAQ covers several points that arise around a sale. Geauga County has no tract (geographical) indexing, and only the indexes of recorded documents are online, so a full copy of an old deed means a copy request. Copies made by the public cost ten cents a page, while a copy made with staff help is two dollars a page.

  • Releases and assignments do not need a legal description, but they do carry the $4.00 marginal notation fee.
  • Soldier discharge records (DD214) are recorded, and a recorded discharge is what the office uses to issue a Veterans ID card.
  • Blank forms are not sold. For one, the FAQ points you to a title company, an attorney or an office supply store.
  • The office will not search the title for you, and it will not notarize or give legal advice.

A shortage or overage on the check sends the document back unrecorded, so call (440) 279-2020 with the page count if you are unsure. The mailing address and the delivery address are the same, 231 Main Street, Suite 1-C, so a courier and the postal service reach one door.

What do Geauga County's housing numbers look like to a seller?

The 2020 Census put Geauga's population at 95,397, and the July 2025 estimate is 95,676. Owner-occupancy is 87.2 percent, the middle-of-the-road owned home is valued at $331,100, and household income has a median of $107,860. Builders pulled 180 permits there in 2025.

Streams that feed the Cuyahoga, Chagrin and Grand rivers start in this county's 400 square miles of land. An average year brings more than 42 inches of precipitation to most of it, more than any other northern Ohio county, so drainage and basements deserve attention before you list.

Chardon, Burton, Middlefield, South Russell and Hunting Valley are the municipalities, and the townships include Bainbridge, Munson, Russell and Newbury. In November 2024 voters dissolved the Village of Aquilla, and a transition board oversees the change.

What are the total charges to record a deed in Geauga County?

At the Recorder, plan on $34.00 for two pages, $8.00 for each extra one and $20.00 more for a non-standard deed. The Auditor bills $4.00 per $1,000 of value and $0.50 per parcel on its own.

Do I need the County Engineer for a Geauga County deed?

Yes, for paper filings. The Engineer reviews and approves the legal description with an original stamp at no fee, usually within 2 to 3 business days. Legal descriptions sent through electronic recording are the exception.

Where is the Geauga County Recorder located?

Find it at 231 Main Street, Suite 1-C, Chardon, Ohio 44024, or ring (440) 279-2020. The County Auditor is in Suite 1-A of the same building.

Will the Recorder search the title to my house?

No. The Recorder's FAQ says state law prohibits the office from doing title searches. Try the online index of recorded documents, or hire a title company or an attorney.

The Recorder lists a same-day turnaround. Mailed deeds come back to you after recording in the self-addressed stamped envelope you include, and an electronic recording is returned when it is recorded.

Where do I take a deed to be recorded in Hamilton County?

Go to Room 205 at 138 East Court Street in Cincinnati. The office admits the public from 7:30 AM until 4:00 PM on weekdays, though the desk that accepts new filings shuts at 3:30 PM.

Mail goes to the same room. Include a stamped envelope bearing your own address, and expect the office to return the recorded deed in about two or three business days. Blank forms are not sold there, so a deed has to come from a lawyer, a closing agent or your own drafting.

How big is Hamilton County, and who owns homes there?

Hamilton County fills the southwest corner of Ohio, with Cincinnati as its seat. After the 2020 count it ranked third in population among Ohio counties. Of its 413 square miles, about 406 are land, folded into hills where the Great Miami, the Little Miami and Mill Creek meet the Ohio River valley.

Territorial officials created the county in 1790, the second in the Northwest Territory, and that early start explains why the Recorder's site can display scanned deed books from 1794 onward.

Which Hamilton County office sees a deed first?

The Auditor comes first and the Recorder second. By mail, the Recorder takes a conveyance only with the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps already on it, and staff will not carry the deed through those stops on your behalf.

  1. Have the deed drafted, signed and acknowledged.
  2. Fill out the conveyance form: DTE Form 100 when value is declared, DTE Form 100 EX when an exemption applies.
  3. Bring the deed, forms and fee to Room 304, the Auditor's Transfer Desk, on the same street.
  4. Take the stamped deed to Room 205, adding a return envelope if you want it mailed back.

The Transfer Desk keeps the same weekday hours, but paperwork arriving after 3:20 PM is held until the next business day. Because that cutoff comes before the Recorder's 3:30 PM close, leave time for the Auditor stop in the morning.

What are the recording fees at the Hamilton County Recorder?

Two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease or power of attorney cost $34.00 together, with $8.00 for every further page. The office adds that the Ohio General Assembly, and not the county, sets these amounts.

ServiceAmount listed

Amounts come from the Recorder's fee schedule and FAQ. Underpaid filings come back unrecorded, while overpaid filings are recorded and the difference refunded. Cards carry an added charge of $2.00 for debit, or the larger of $2.00 and 2.39% for credit.

How much does the Hamilton County Auditor collect at transfer?

Certain transfers skip the price-based charges. Form DTE 100 EX names reasons such as gifts within a marriage or from parent to child, passage to an heir or devisee, and deeds that merely fix an earlier recorded one. Two exemption boxes always call for an affidavit of facts: security for a debt, and a no-money transfer that is not a gift.

Other forms may join the packet. A seller who had the homestead reduction last year or this year files DTE Form 101, and land with an agricultural use valuation calls for DTE Form 102.

Does Hamilton County still have registered (Torrens) land?

Registered land is no longer a separate track in Hamilton County. The Board of Commissioners passed Resolution 25 on August 6, 2014 to abolish it, and since November 10, 2015 any registered land document is recorded in the traditional system at the standard $34.00 and $8.00 rates.

No new certificate of title is issued under that change. A preparer should cite the existing certificate of title as the prior instrument until the parcel has changed hands. The county notes it held more registered land than any other Ohio county, and it has put millions of registered land images online.

Tell your title agent early if your parcel was ever registered. State law bars adverse possession claims against registered land, so such a parcel's history deserves a closer look.

What older records can I view from the Hamilton County Recorder online?

The Recorder's home page opens a historic search that goes well past modern deeds. It lists grantor and grantee deed indexes for 1914 to 1988, deed books from 1794 to 1903, mortgage and mortgage release books from 1794 into the early 1900s, and mechanic lien, lease and power of attorney documents from the same early period.

  • Cemetery lot documents (1794 to 1934).
  • Church and organization documents (1794 to 1919).
  • Veteran discharge records (1794 to 1965).
  • Plat maps, a 1913 Cincinnati street index and a 1824 map of the Symmes survey.

These help a seller trace how a very old parcel was first conveyed, and they help a title examiner find an old easement or lien that never got released.

What page format does the Recorder expect on a deed?

A single statute, ORC 317.114, sets the page standard statewide, and the Recorder's FAQ links to its standardization guidelines. Off-standard deeds are still taken, with $10 plus another $10 added.

  • Type at least size ten, in dark ink without highlighter.
  • Sheets from letter size up to legal length.
  • One inch of white space at the sides and the foot.
  • Three inches left clear at the head of page one, plus one and a half inches on later pages, for county endorsements.

Releases and assignments must carry a full legal description under ORC 5301.46, and a Hamilton County deed that describes the land differently from the last recorded deed may need a boundary survey approved by the County Engineer before the Auditor will transfer it.

Does Hamilton County offer a deed fraud alert?

Yes. The Recorder's Real Estate Fraud Alert is a free notification service. If a document is recorded under an identity you are watching, you receive an email.

The office's online search, called Acclaim, lets anyone browse the index and document images without paying. For owners who live out of town or hold inherited property, signing up costs nothing and gives early warning of an unexpected filing against the parcel.

More questions about Hamilton County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Will the Hamilton County Recorder write my deed for me?

No. Blank forms are not sold there and staff cannot do searches or title work. Have a lawyer or closing agent draft the deed.

Can a deed be mailed to the Hamilton County Recorder?

Yes, once the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps are on it. Add a prepaid return envelope with your own address so the recorded deed can find its way home.

When does the Hamilton County recording desk shut?

At 3:30 PM, half an hour before the office itself closes. Items handed to the Auditor's Transfer Desk after 3:20 PM wait for the next business day.

Is one payment enough for both Hamilton County offices?

No. Each office bills separately: conveyance and transfer charges go to the Auditor, and the recording fee goes to the Recorder.

Must a new owner in Hamilton County record the deed?

In practice yes. ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent toward a later good-faith buyer who knew nothing of it, leaving the new owner's title exposed until the Recorder indexes the deed.

Northwest Ohio's Hancock County spans 531 square miles of land and counts Findlay as both seat and largest city. According to the Recorder's FAQ, the Auditor's conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. A deed that changes ownership stops at the Auditor before the Recorder, and the two offices coordinate so the transfer and recording line up.

ORC 319.202 has the buyer or the buyer's representative file the value statement. It counts the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage and vendor's lien included, as the value, and it forbids willfully falsifying that figure. An exempt transfer needs only a statement of the reason.

If the land had a homestead reduction or an agricultural valuation, ask the Auditor which extra forms apply, since the statute has the buyer question the seller on both.

What risk comes with an unrecorded Hancock County deed?

A deed left unrecorded loses ground to a later buyer. ORC 5301.25 sends deeds to the recorder of the county where the land lies, and until that happens they are fraudulent against a subsequent good-faith purchaser with no knowledge of them.

The same statute deals with surveys. When land being conveyed was surveyed, the Auditor requires the surveyor's name in the deed, in a line reading "A survey of this property was made by" and then the name.

For a seller here, a tidy deed history keeps a title search short, while a gap can delay closing.

  • Plats 24 by 36 inches: $50 a page.

  • Township zoning resolutions: $50, and zoning amendments: $20.

Those figures come from the Recorder's January 2025 schedule.

How do Hancock County's townships show up in deed descriptions?

The county began in 1828 as Findlay Township alone, with Amanda and Welfare (now Delaware) added that April. Jackson came in 1829, Liberty and Marion in December 1830, and Big Lick, Blanchard and Van Buren in 1831. Washington, Union and Eagle were laid out in 1832, Cass and Portage in 1833, Pleasant in 1835, Orange in 1836, Madison in 1840 and Allen in 1850.

In 1845 part of the southeast corner went to the newly formed Wyandot County. Farmland outside Findlay is often described by township, so deeds for those parcels will cite these units. Check that your new deed repeats the description from the deed you received.

Can I look up Hancock County land records myself?

The Recorder's online search holds documents recorded and imaged from January 1, 1985 to the present, and historical indexes can be viewed online as well. Enter names last name first, such as Doe John, and enter companies as they normally appear.

A search cannot be run by parcel number at the Recorder's office. You need the owner's name and the legal description. If you lack either one, start at the Hancock County Auditor's website to find the owner and parcel details, then return to the Recorder.

The county is indexed alphabetically online only for 1985 to the present, and anything earlier has to be searched in the office. The Recorder will also provide copies by phone, in person or through the website.

Can I e-record a deed in Hancock County?

Yes. Electronic filing is accepted for every document type, including deeds that must pass the Auditor's conveyance step. The office works with four outside submission services.

E-recording suits title firms, lenders and law offices best. A homeowner can simply ask whoever handles the closing whether the deed will be sent electronically.

Will the Hancock County Recorder add or remove a name on my deed?

Not without a new deed. The Recorder says adding or removing someone, or changing a name, takes a newly prepared deed, and the office only records documents. It suggests an attorney or title office to prepare it.

Who holds my original deed after I pay off my mortgage in Hancock County?

Neither the Recorder nor your bank holds the original deed during the loan. You should get it back shortly after closing, so contact the attorney or title office that handled the sale. If it is lost, the Recorder can make a copy.

Does the Hancock County Recorder provide blank deed forms?

By 4:00 pm. The office stays open until 4:30 pm, but recording for the day ends at 4:00 pm and later filings are recorded on the next business day.

Splits and combinations of parcels need Auditor preapproval and a minimum of three days. Those requests are made by form and emailed, since they are no longer taken in person.

What does the Harrison County Recorder charge?

The Recorder's fee page prints $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after that, citing ORC 317.32. It also explains that half of all recording fees go to the state for the Ohio Housing Trust Fund.

ItemFee printed by the Recorder
Recording, first two pages$34.00
Recording, each additional page$8.00
Marginal reference by separate instrument$4.00
Certified photocopy$2.00 per page, plus $1.00 for the seal
Photocopy of a record, from the overview page$2.00 per page
Plat, minimum fee$40.00

Source: Harrison County Recorder fee page and office overview. State law has been amended since that page was written, and ORC 317.32 now permits a document preservation surcharge of up to $5. Call the office to confirm the total before you write a check. The overview page says veterans are entitled to free certified copies.

What do the abbreviations on Harrison County deeds mean?

The Auditor's transfer page lists common deed types with short codes that appear in county records. Knowing them helps you read a chain of title.

  • WD is a General Warranty Deed, and QC is a Quit Claim Deed.
  • ED is an Executor's Deed, AD an Administrator's Deed and FD a Fiduciary Deed.
  • TD is a Trustee's Deed, and SD is a Sheriff's Deed.
  • SV is a Survivorship Deed, and TO is a Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit.
  • CD is a Corrected Deed or re-recording, and MD is a Mineral Deed.
  • AF is an Affidavit, AT an Affidavit Relating to Title, and RW a Right of Way or Easement.

A seller who inherited the house will often hold an ED, AD or TO in the chain. A buyer's title agent will want that document and the preceding ones in order.

What else is in Harrison County besides farmland and wells?

The Conotton Creek Trail, a paved rails-to-trails path of 11.4 miles, runs along Conotton Creek from Bowerston to Jewett in the northern part of the county. The Recorder's office also serves on the county records commission, which decides how long county records are kept and when they may be disposed of.

The Recorder collects document fees for the county's general fund and each year notifies the county commissioners and township trustees of their duty to file zoning resolutions, maps and amendments. Those zoning filings can matter to a seller with land in one of the 15 townships.

Do mineral rights show up on Harrison County deeds?

They can. Harrison County sits over the Utica shale, which drew attention as a tight oil zone, and the county's history includes oil finds near Jewett in 1895 and the Scio area in 1898. Because of that, a deed may reserve or convey minerals separately from the surface.

The Auditor's list of common deed types includes a Mineral Deed, along with the General Warranty Deed, Quit Claim Deed, Survivorship Deed, Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit and others. The state recorders' fee table also lists a claim to preserve mineral interests as a recordable item.

  • Ask the title company whether minerals were reserved in an earlier deed.
  • Ask whether any oil and gas lease is of record on the parcel.
  • Make sure the new deed states exactly what is conveyed.

Where can I search Harrison County property records online?

The Recorder lists an online records search through Kofile's CountyFusion and a newer cloud search at harrison.oh.publicsearch.us. A Property Alert service is also listed on the Recorder's page.

If you ask for copies by mail, the Recorder charges $2.00 per page, and payment is due before the copies are sent. To find a record, give the owner's name, the volume and page, or the subdivision, lot, township, range and section.

More questions about Harrison County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How long does Harrison County preapproval take?

A minimum of four days. The Map Office, Auditor and Recorder all review the unsigned copy before returning it with any needed changes.

What does Harrison County charge per thousand dollars of price?

The Auditor lists $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, without rounding, plus $0.50 per parcel, payable by check or cash.

What time does the Harrison County Recorder stop recording?

4:15 p.m. Documents received after that until 4:30 p.m. are recorded the next business day.

Does the Harrison County Recorder supply deed forms?

No. The Recorder's office does not furnish forms. The Auditor adds that it does not prepare deeds and recommends a legal representative for a transfer.

Can veterans get copies of discharge papers in Harrison County?

Yes. The Recorder's overview says veterans are entitled to free certified copies, and certified copies of DD214s go to funeral homes.
